MilanNews write that the club ‘have Cagliari to thank for that May day at San Siro’. It’s paradoxical, following an initial instinctive reaction: how can Milan hosting Ferencvaros be better than facing PSG, Barcelona ​​or Manchester City on a magical Champions League night?

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Well, considering how Massimiliano Allegri is doing with Napoli, there is a compelling case that it was necessary pain. The report explained the thesis.

Allegri’s decline began on 15 March 2026, the day of the 1-0 defeat away against Lazio after he won the derby thanks to Pervis Estupinan’s goal. It takes us to 4 November 2026, the date of Porto 4-1 Napoli, that latest terrible result from the coach.

It seems that bad results constant tension in the dressing room have followed Max in the past few months. In this block of 20 matches between Milan and Napoli, Allegri’s difficulty is evident, with a decidedly negative record of 11 defeats against only six wins and three draws.

Furthermore, 31 goals conceded in 20 matches is enormous for teams historically led by a pragmatic and defensive manager like the Livorno-born manager. Essentially, since that derby won with that surreal goal from Estupinan, ‘Allegrismo’ has only meant disasters.

The feeling is that if Milan had celebrated their return to the Champions League they would have kept Allegri, but in the long run they would have wasted another year chasing a style of football and a way of managing the club that no longer seems viable.

Less than 24 hours after the Cagliari game, there was a clear-out of the management as Gerry Cardinale saw fit to launch yet another revolution. It takes time and patience, but perhaps it’s better this way, to feel like something is genuinely being built towards.

Without Giorgio Furlani as CEO, the club will be entrusted to a competent and experienced Head of Football (likely to be Markus Krösche, a director with obvious pedigree). With Ruben Amorim at the helm, we can expect to see a more modern and entertaining style.

There are of course inconsistencies to iron out, and the squad must be improved, but we must question what would have been lost had Cagliari not made history that night at San Siro.

The William Saliba Arsenal boost comes at a crucial time. Saliba can use the November international break to build up his fitness after missing out on France’s latest squad.

Arteta confirmed that the defender had returned to full training ahead of Arsenal’s Champions League meeting with Slavia Prague. He also completed 45 minutes in a behind-closed-doors-friendly last week as he stepped up his recovery.

However, Saliba did not feature in the 2-1 victory. Arteta included him in the matchday squad for the first time this season, but the Frenchman remained an unused substitute.

It means he was not selected by Zinedine Zidane for France’s Nations League games against Italy and Turkey. This gives Arsenal a chance to continue working on his recovery. He will not be travelling for international games or playing in competitive matches.

Saliba has not featured since he suffered a back injury during France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain in July. Arteta has had to find alternatives in central defence in the early stages of the campaign.

This means he will be able to continue to be monitored by the club at their London Colney training ground. He won’t be able to return to play in international games ahead of his first appearance for the club.

Arsenal will be hoping that he can use the extra time to get himself ready for the next set of games, including a trip to Newcastle before playing Borussia Dortmund and Manchester City at home.

In Arsenal transfer news, Arsenal could approach the January transfer window with a different focus after Fabrizio Romano revealed that Mikel Arteta has no intention of weakening his defensive options.

Piero Hincapié has been linked with a move to Barcelona. There have been reports that a deal could be done involving Alejandro Balde, but Romano expects the Ecuadorian to stay at Emirates Stadium.

Arsenal have been strengthening their defensive department under Arteta. Hincapié only made the switch permanently from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer after joining on loan.

Despite competition, the 24-year-old is a key player in Arteta’s plans. His versatility to play in either a centre back or left back role gives Arteta a valuable option.

However, we can also gain insight into where Arsenal should target their recruitment from Romano’s latest comments. Instead of changing their defensive options, it could be an opportunity to improve their attacking options.

Despite competition, the 24-year-old is a key player in Arteta’s plans. His versatility to play in either a centre back or left back role gives Arteta a valuable option.

However, we can also gain insight into where Arsenal should target their recruitment from Romano’s latest comments. Instead of changing their defensive options, it could be an opportunity to improve their attacking options.

However, Arsenal have little incentive to let him leave halfway through the season, as losing a two-in-one defender will cause problems for Arteta, given how much they need to do in multiple competitions.

Romano’s comments suggest that Arsenal are happy with their existing defensive unit and don’t want to cause any disruption to their balance. He also suggested that Hincapié is an important player for them, meaning he’s unlikely to leave in January.

That leaves Barcelona needing to explore alternative targets if they want to strengthen their backline. A deal involving Balde and Hincapié does not currently appear to be a realistic option.

The more interesting part of Romano’s report is Arsenal’s potential business at the other end of the field.

He feels they will be looking to make a move if the right attacking player comes up for grabs. But he doesn’t think they will make a signing just because they can in January.

This highlights the issues clubs face with mid-season transfers. Often selling clubs will be unwilling to lose key players, and finding suitable replacements can be tough.

As such, Arsenal are likely to look at the market to see what they can do. However, it looks like there could still be a forward brought in.

This is an important distinction. The point being made here is that whilst there is speculation around one particular player, Romano has indicated that Arsenal can strengthen their attacking options. This is not to say that any particular move is happening.

If Arteta keeps Hincapié, then Arsenal will maintain their defensive stability and possibly gain another option in attack.

Over the next few weeks we will get a better understanding of what is available to them. But for now it looks like Arsenal are not keen to lose Hincapié but will look to strengthen their attacking options if the right deal comes along.

#2053. Arsenal 1-0 Hull City: Martin Ødegaard rescues Gunners with late winner at the Emirates

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal needed a moment of quality from their captain to overcome Hull City and claim a narrow 1-0 Premier League victory at the Emirates Stadium.

Martin Ødegaard scored in the 72nd minute as the hosts struggled to break down a resolute Hull side. It was much like I expected in my match preview, as Arsenal had to work hard to win this game.

The result gives them an extended lead at the top of the table. Ahead of Manchester City’s clash with Nottingham Forest. However, Mikel Arteta will be aware that his team did not play well in this game. It was far from a walk in the park.

Hull arrived at London looking to play an attacking game. Jakirovic’s side were well organised and looked to launch quick counter attacks.

They did have some positive moments in the first half, but Arsenal struggled to get into their attacking rhythm. Kai Havertz couldn’t capitalise on one good chance created by Ødegaard.

The hosts were hopeful of taking the lead after Havertz fell to the ground in the box after being pulled back by Nobel Mendy.

However, referee Farai Hallam’s initial decision was overturned after a VAR review showed Havertz was offside earlier in the attack, so Arsenal’s penalty was cancelled.

Another frustrating moment for the home side, who failed to score during the first half, despite dominating possession.

Arsenal came out strong after the break. However, Hull were still causing problems. Lewie Coyle was also walking a fine line after a yellow card in the first half and a late challenge on Christos Tzolis.

Arteta made a three-man change on the hour mark, bringing on Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino for Havertz and Declan Rice. Six minutes later he brought on Eberechi Eze and Piero Hincapié.

The breakthrough came from Madueke, forcing Konstantinos Tzolakis into action. The Hull keeper couldn’t hold his shot, and Ødegaard was quickest to react, scoring from the rebound.

The captain’s strike took the frustration out of Arsenal’s efforts and was a reward for their perseverance. It also provided another vital moment for the Norwegian. He’s had a tough campaign so far due to injuries.

Despite going behind, Hull never gave up in their search for an equaliser. However, Arsenal held on to their lead.

Arsenal dominated the game with 67% of possession and 21 shots, compared to just seven for Hull. Tzolakis put in a number of key interventions to keep the scoreline respectable.

Although they weren’t at their best, Arsenal were able to perform in the key moments of the game. Ødegaard’s goal meant that the Gunners earned three points and are sitting top of the Premier League heading into the international break.

#2052. Motherwell ace feeling 21 again as he embraces senior role

Motherwell striker Callum Hendry aims to be a key player on and off the park after getting back to fitness.

Hendry made his first appearance of the season in Saturday’s 1-0 win over St Mirren following knee surgery, having come back from a four-month lay-off in April last season.

Speaking ahead of Saturday’s trip to face Dundee United, the former St Johnstone player said: “I sorted out the double hernia and then playing and training consistently probably covered the injury that I had.

“At the start of summer I started running again and I had really bad, really angry tendonitis, so it just needed fixing. I got the operation and I feel good now and hopefully I can put it behind me.

“I’m very optimistic. The more minutes I get, the fitter I’ll get, the sharper I’ll get. And I’ve seen that the team’s creating a lot of chances.”

Hendry, Paul McGinn and Oscar Priestman all returned off the bench against Saints to give the squad a lift.

“I’ve actually felt like there’s a bit of a glow around training having us back, because it’s such a tight-knit group,” the 28-year-old said. “It was just nice for us all to come back for the same game, and win it.

“The culture hasn’t changed, which I think is important, because we created such a good culture last year and we’ve kept it somehow, which is quite rare for such an overhaul of players.

“There’s a few younger lads in there, different changing room really, but still got the same feel to it. The boys are still close.

“It’s important that you stick together. They have had to stick together through some tough results the last couple of months where they haven’t really deserved them.

“I’ve had a few boys speak to me and ask me for advice, more this time than the last few seasons.

“I still feel 21, but my body tells me different sometimes. But it’s nice to be that guy because I always leaned on the older pros when I was younger.”

#2050. Aston Villa news: Unai Emery reveals latest on contract talks ahead of Man United showdown

By Darren Plant | 06 Nov 2026 17:37

Aston Villa manager Unai Emery has admitted that discussions over a new contract have been "very positive".

Emery and his squad are currently preparing to face Manchester United in the Premier League on Sunday.

There had been the potential for a huge sub-plot, with the Red Devils' hierarchy known to be admirers of the Spaniard.

However, Emery will take his place in the Villa dugout at the Theatre of Dreams having made it clear that he has no interest in replacing Michael Carrick.

Meanwhile, Villa revealed earlier this week that they have held extensive talks with the 54-year-old over plans for the long-term future.

Speaking at a press conference, Emery hinted that it may only be a matter of time before he extends his contract past 2029.

He told reporters: "I had a good meeting with [chairman] Nassef Sawiris, very positive, so let's talk next week, trying to get everything we spoke about together in a deal.

"My vision is to keep our consistency and how we are improving, how we are building a lot of things positively; being strong, keeping it consistent in our process. It's a huge challenge, but the club is involved in it.

"After speaking with us last year, they decided to build a new stand, adding more supporters in Villa Park. It's one clear step forward to getting better.

"We are increasing our budget each year, increasing our revenue through our performance, playing in Europe, improving players, selling players, then buying young, talented players.

"This is the process of the vision we should keep in our future."

For all of the recent positivity at Villa Park, Emery's side have gone three matches without a win in all competitions.

With Villa already four points adrift of fourth place in the Premier League table, they can ill-afford more dropped points against Man United.

Carrick's side, who are deemed to be in disarray, can move to within two points of Villa with a second high-profile triumph this week, after they beat Roma on Tuesday.

#2048. Chelsea news: Xabi Alonso reacts to Cole Palmer's England squad omission, Thomas Tuchel comments

By Darren Plant | 06 Nov 2026 17:37

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has suggested that he has little interest in Cole Palmer's ongoing situation with England.

With five goals and three assists from 11 appearances in 2026-27, the 24-year-old can be relatively pleased with his start to the season.

However, after withdrawing from England's squad for their September and October fixtures due to either a minor injury or to manage his workload, the playmaker is in the bad books of Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel.

After leaving Palmer out of his latest squad on Friday, the German reiterated that the player is paying the price for 'missed opportunities' to impress.

Despite the perceived disappointment of one of his key players, Alonso hinted at a press conference on Friday that he does not get himself involved with national team matters.

He told reporters: "No. We have not spoken about that. We have been talking about our game on Sunday."

When pushed on whether there are any regrets from Palmer over withdrawing from the last squad, the Spaniard added: "We haven't spoken about that.

"We are focussed on our things, on Chelsea things and how to do better and how to help him and how he can become more and more influential on the game. Those are our topics to talk."

Having continued to be pressed on the subject, Alonso reiterated: "We speak about Chelsea. We have enough on our plate. My impact area is my control area and what we talk about."

The assumption is that Palmer will feel disappointed having missed out on another opportunity to represent England.

Despite the mixed reports that came out about the reasoning being his withdrawal last time, Tuchel has clearly been left unimpressed.

To many, it will feel unusual that Alonso has not spoken to Palmer about matters relating to England.

Even if he challenged Palmer to use it as motivation when with Chelsea, Alonso being dismissive about the subject comes across as a surprise.

#2046. Fulham 1 Newcastle 1 A very good away display and only disappointment not all 3 points

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Fulham 1 Newcastle 1 – Saturday 7 November 2026 3pm

A pretty even open start to the match and the first big moment a good save after a quarter of an hour by Hornicek from Bobb.

A few minutes later and Barnes came close to opening the scoring, he flicked on Murphy’s cross at the near post but Leno saving.

Just after the half hour mark two huge moments.

Harvey Barnes released behind the Fulham defence and running from the halfway line he did everything right, got the keeper to commit but as he swept the ball over him it hit Leno’s head and out for a corner.

A short corner taken and when the cross came in it was Dan Burn from close in, the referee though swiftly disallowing it, seemingly for a foul by Wissa.

Hornicek making a few saves in the opening half and another one just before half-time as he pushed away a strong strike.

A couple of minutes after the break and a sweeping move saw Dedic feed Wissa, squared it to Barnes just inside the penalty area and one of those where you expect it to hit the back of the net.

Similar to his goal at Palace but a bit more difficult and not as central, this time he swept it just past the right hand post.

On 70 minutes a very good team move and sweet low cross from Dedic that Osula just couldn’t reach for a tap in.

Sean Steur with a very good performance linking play and subbed off with 15 minutes left.

An end to end game and with 13 minutes of normal time remaining a low shot from sub Willock bounced awkwardly for Leno but he grabbed at the second attempt.

A loose Fulham pass intercepted by Jacob Murphy and cutting between two defenders a super left footed 25 yarder giving Leno no chance!

A couple of minutes after the restart, 1-1.

Thiaw unlucky as he deflected the ball to Muniz in the box and it was a clever finish by the Fulham player BUT it needed a deflection off Burn to give Hornicek no chance.

A few minutes to go and Lewis Hall pops up in the box, plenty of goal to aim at but his low right foot shot just too close to Leno who got an outstretched hand to it.

Into added time and when a free-kick cleared to just outside the box, a volley from a Fulham player brilliantly saved by Hornicek.

The referee Rob Jones was absolutely shocking, as usual. Time after time Fulham getting the decisions.

I thought it was cruel on Matthias Jaissle and his players that they didn’t pick up all three points. Not a lot in it but Newcastle the better team in the second half and deserved to edge it.

A very decent away performance though and fair play to the NUFC Head Coach and his team.

#2044. Fonseca revisits bitter Milan exit: “I didn’t even get a phone call”

Paulo Fonseca has strongly hinted at being unhappy with how his experience at AC Milan came to such a sudden end.

Fonseca joined Milan ahead of the 2024-25 season, tasked with replacing Stefano Pioli who had won a Scudetto and reached a Champions League semi-final. However, he did not even last until the end of the year before being sacked after a draw with Roma.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It wasn’t a very well-kept secret that the Portuguese was under pressure, and it didn’t take long until Sergio Conceicao replaced him in what seemed to be a manoeuvre orchestrated mainly by agent Jorge Mendes.

Fast-forwarding to the past week, Fonseca abruptly left Lyon in order to return to Portugal with Sporting CP, with whom he signed a contract until 30 June 2030. He takes the place of Rui Borges, and during the press conference (via Calciomercato.com) he revealed some details.

“I think there was a phone call. It happened around the time the rumours started circulating that Rui had refused to speak to me.

“Yesterday I had the pleasure of speaking with him: it was a very open and honest conversation, between two coaches who perfectly understand, without any hypocrisy, what moments like these mean.

“We spoke at length, very pleasantly, with great mutual respect and admiration, as I’ve said before. I didn’t just speak with Rui, but also with his assistant, Tiago, whom I’ve known for a long time. Sometimes controversy arises when, in reality, things are completely normal.

“I can tell you this story. I was at Milan, we were playing against Roma, and the coach who would replace me had already been hired [Conceiçao]. The next day I had to quickly clear out my room and locker because the new coach wanted to come in.

“And you know what? I didn’t even get a phone call, but there was no need. In football, these situations are part of the game, and I didn’t take it personally. We must understand, without hypocrisy, that these processes are natural.”

#2043. 3 Positives and 3 Negatives to take from Fulham 1 Newcastle 1

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Saturday’s match ended Fulham 1 Newcastle 1.

Ahead of each game we ask one of our writers to come up with three positives and three negatives following the game.

Plenty to talk about after this Fulham one…

A match that saw Newcastle United take the lead with a stunning long range Jacob Murphy left foot stunner.

Only for Fulham to deny United all three points only a couple of minutes after the restart.

On this occasion it is ‘Matt Busby said to Joe Harvey…’ with the positives and negatives:

I criticised Hornicek on Monday; it was deserved, after he let the ball squirm under him to gift Thierno Barry his goal.

Five days later at Craven Cottage, the young Czech is probably our MOTM, a string of decent saves from Oscar Bobb, Josh King, Timothy Castagne, before the pick of the lot, diving full stretch to deny Ryan Sessegnon in injury time and preserve United’s point.

Although it was very frustrating to concede less than three minutes after Jacob Murphy had put us ahead, we could have still conspired to lose this one, so a point is a point and after Monday’s debacle, we needed to limit our losses.

That’s four games in London this season; three wins and a draw with only one goal conceded.

That was a peach of a strike from Jacob Murphy in the 80th minute and it should have delivered us all three points.

Not only did he score that cracker, I thought Murphy was our best outfield player today, responsible for creating two big chances for Barnes and Burn, whose disallowed goal should have stood in my opinion.

Murphy also did some decent defensive work, tracking back in support of Dedic, so it’s a toss up between him and the keeper for my MOTM award.

Not only did our lead take less than three minutes to dismantle, it was the manner in which it was lost that was so annoying.

Unnecessary panicking, unable to clear our lines and an awful deflection all conspiring against us. We still look very brittle at the back.

I thought pairing these two in the centre of the park was a no-brainer and long overdue.

In some respects, I was a little surprised to see Matthias Jaissle agreeing with me today, but when the team was announced, the German had seemingly taken heed.

Unfortunately, neither was able to stamp their authority on the game and the so-called double pivot didn’t work out; Fulham dominated possession and our transition from defence into attack was very sluggish.

It wasn’t a surprise that both were replaced but I don’t think Jaissle should give up on this pairing based solely on today.

He may well be, although he wasn’t at fault for their equaliser, just like he can’t be blamed for what looks like such poor recruitment over the past couple of windows.

What concerns me about this manager is that he doesn’t seem capable of getting a tune out of his players and where is Aladji Bamba?

#2042. ‘A step in the right direction…’ Matthias Jaissle speaks out after Fulham 1 Newcastle 1

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Matthias Jaissle watched on as the match ended Fulham 1 Newcastle 1.

A stunning long range left foot effort from Jacob Murphy looked to have won it for United in the 80th minute.

Only for Fulham to swiftly equalise with the help of a couple of deflections, helping to get the ball to goalscorer Muniz and then his shot taking a tough off Burn to give Hornicek no chance.

Matthias Jaissle speaking to BBC Sport: “A step in the right direction after the last performance. That’s something we can really build on. I think there were occasions also to win that game. Of course, the disallowed goal, a soft one, I would say. I see it different then also a big chance at the end. Then you should go home with three points but one point and a performance is something we can work on.”

Matthias Jaissle on Jacob Murphy’s superb long range goal: “A brilliant goal and in general a great performance. Really solid defensively, he did his job, and offensive-wise, with such a goal, a great evening for him.”

Matthias Jaissle asked about the yellow card he got late on: “Not understandable really. I was shouting at my player that he should get up because if we can lose him for one minute at a decisive moment of the game, yeah, he should get up. Only when he is really injured can I understand it. The referee then gives me the yellow card. That’s strange.”

Mattias Jaissle on Dan Burn’s disallowed goal: “Do you think it’s a foul? In the Premier League? No.”

Matthias Jaissle on the international break: “It is now time to reflect and recharge also with a long season ahead of us, then pull out the things we need to improve and there are a couple of aspects. But today showed a clear direction in the right way so we can build on that.”

Interesting to read through these BBC Sport ‘neutrals’ comments, following on from Newcastle United drawing 1-1 at Fulham.

A very open match with plenty of action at both ends of the pitch.

Newcastle United though with the clearer chances and the better team in the second half.

Jacob Murphy with a superb left foot long range strike that looked to have won it on 80 minutes, only for Fulham to hit back with an equaliser three minutes later as United failed to clear their lines and a couple of deflections aided Fulham.

Referee Rob Jones was woeful as usual with Newcastle United, looking to give Fulham as many decisions as possible.

Four games in London for Matthias Jaissle in all competitions and still unbeaten, three wins and a draw in the capital.

Always interesting to hear the neutral perspectives, as well as the perspectives of fans of Fulham, Newcastle United and…Sunderland.

The BBC Sport readers comments from neutrals…

‘I thought the ref was very consistent as he gave Fulham every 50/50 call including the Wissa incident to deny Burn his goal. Then after getting in the way of a Newcastle pass he gave the ball to Fulham. Astonishing.’

‘Funny result considering the Fulham scorer should’ve been sent off for elbowing Thiaw within seconds of entering the pitch.

‘I like Newcastle as a neutral but can forsee a battle at the wrong end of the PL. No consistency again and never know what you are going to get.’

‘A point earned. Great performance from the travelling toon army. Not impressed with the refereeing which seemed very inconsistent.’

‘Again another game in which newcastle had more than enough chances to score, at least this time Murphy came up with something. I think a game is going to come when they actually take most of the chances and score a hat full, hopefully that will help them kick on for the rest of the season.’

‘(Sunderland fan) We’ll be very lucky to stay up this season.’

I was at the match . Fair result. We were the better team 1st half,NUFC had the better of the 2nd. That’s 4 matches in the Prem unbeaten now. Onwards and upwards !’

‘No wonder Newcastle fans are switching to archery!

‘Newcastle manager has got to go …schar on in 84 minute , miley and willock ? Not game winning subs there. #2037. Is one point away from home ever a bad point? Fulham 1 Newcastle 1

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

In answer to the question above, the outcome at Craven Cottage definitely felt as if Newcastle United had dropped two rather than gained one, perhaps because we conceded a late equaliser.

Compared with May’s encounter, in what proved to be Eddie Howe’s final Premier League game as our head coach, the performance was much better, though still a long way below what I believe is possible.

Before kick-off I would have taken the draw. I said as much to a Fulham fan on the walk from Putney Bridge Tube station through Bishops Park. An American, she lives in Clapham and last season needed to choose a London club to support when her most recent serious relationship ended. No way would she continue to cheer for his team!

Her choice of Fulham was based partly on the club’s questionable claim to be the oldest in the capital. When I pointed out that in 147 years Fulham had never won a big trophy (domestic or European) she replied that she followed football for the fun, not the glory. An admirable attitude . . .

We shook hands and wished each other good luck at 2.30pm on the corner of the Riverside and Putney End stands. Another random conversation to add to the collection.

On the train up from Brighton I had quizzed an Arsenal fan, who was taking his two sons to The Emirates for the game against Hull.

What was his verdict on Bruno G? Why wasn’t our former captain a regular starter?

“We rotate nearly every match. Arteta picks him against teams who play a low block. I like Bruno because he’s always looking forward, trying to create. Lewis-Skelly is preferred in European games, which are more open. We also have Eze, who is probably 13th on the team sheet.”

A veritable wealth of riches for the title-winning manager.

Not that the Arsenal fan on the train had been confident last season, fearing the recent history of blowing their chances was likely to be repeated again.

Hadn’t Arsenal succeeded at last despite Arteta, rather than because of him, I suggested. The style of football was efficient rather than attractive. When we went to The Emirates in April, with Man City hot on Arsenal’s heels, the tension was palpable. An Eze cracker from a short corner routine saw them home that day. Another 1-0 to The Arsenal, just as they managed yesterday against Hull City.

How will they cope against Newcastle 2.0, when they meet at St James’ Park immediately after the international break? If United play to their full potential, with Sean Steur making things tick in midfield and Lewis Hall surging up the wing after quelling attacks, anything is possible. We proved that in the 2024/25 season, when we beat them three times.

Possible but unlikely, because we no longer have Isak and Gordon to fire the bullets supplied by Bruno G. Neither do we have the oh-so-predictable leadership of Howe; predictable as in getting the better of Arteta with pleasing frequency.

We lacked that sort of firepower yesterday. William Osula ran relentlessly to little effect. Yoane Wissa rarely showed the same enthusiasm. The chemistry between them looked embryonic, being charitable. The link play between Amar Dedic and Jacob Murphy on the right flank, between Hall and Harvey Barnes on the left, was sporadic to nonexistent.

When the full-backs advanced, the wide attackers dropped back. That was an understandable response to conceding three goals at Everton, four at Coventry and four at Leeds since mid-September. One consequence was a lot of sideways and backward passing, to the travelling fans’ frustration.

Another consequence was the need for Murphy and Barnes to defend if Fulham regained possession, which they did reasonably well.

With Steur and Nico Gonzalez in the middle of the park, supplemented by their wider teammates, United looked less open.

Matthias Jaissle has been widely blamed for trying to succeed with a two-man midfield. Yesterday the two was often a four, thanks to Dedic and Hall stepping up while Murphy and Barnes stepped back.

Total football it was not. It was, however, more encouraging than a lot of what we have seen in the German’s first three months in charge.

Dan Burn defended solidly and strode forward more than once, trying to make things happen. Malick Thiaw blocked and intercepted impressively from first to last, though his passing was occasionally alarming.

In the interests of research I watched the Everton v Coventry televised game on Friday evening. The referee at the Hill Dickinson was the biggest Homer since Ancient Greece, denying the visitors two penalties and ignoring a handball in Everton’s second goal. VAR refused to get involved just as Howard Webb, head of Pro Ref, wants.

I feared more of the same at Craven Cottage. Rob Jones didn’t disappoint. He was biased with a capital B, favouring the hosts whenever there was an element of doubt and often when there wasn’t. Fouls on visiting players went unpunished, whereas strong challenges by United were often penalised.

The first half contained only a few glimpses of fluid passing from either team. Lukas Hornicek made a couple of spectacular saves, while Barnes forced Bernd Leno to kick away a clever flick from a low Murphy cross. The Fulham keeper also stopped a goal-bound Barnes shot, this time unwittingly with his forehead.

Burn finished smartly at the near post from the resultant corner but the referee deemed Wissa had fouled Timothy Castagne with the sort of routine holding that is usually ignored by the officials.

After the interval United looked more dangerous as they attacked the Putney End that housed the vociferous Toon Army. Barnes cracked a right-foot curler off the outside of the post with Leno nowhere, Wissa was maybe two feet short of a tap-in from another low cross and for a few minutes Fulham struggled to break out of their half.

The replacement of Gonzalez and Wissa by Lewis Miley and Joe Willock on 61 minutes added to the threat. Steur was always available and kept the ball moving in midfield but struggled to recover from a heavy tackle. He made way for Matias Fernandez-Pardo, whose pace immediately unsettled Fulham.

When Murphy seized on a loose pass about 40 yards out on our right flank, he jinked inside, set his sights and with his left boot bent a sizzling shot beyond Leno. Mayhem among the travelling fans!

The cheers and chants were still bouncing around the stadium three minutes later when the equaliser went in. It has been credited to Rodrigo Muniz. Having watched the goal six times on television replays, I reckon Hall kicked the ball onto the Brazilian before it deflected off the diving Burn and into the net past a wrong-footed Hornicek. Perhaps a trip to Specsavers is needed . . .

Neither team were happy to settle for a point. A rapid break down the left led to Hall finding space 12 yards out. Sadly for him and his team, the ball was on his weaker boot and Leno was able to save the low shot.

Fulham could have stolen all three points in stoppage time when Ryan Sessegnon smashed a 20-yarder to Hornicek’s left. The young keeper dived across and parried it to safety, capping what was probably his best game so far for United.

One point gained or two dropped? I favour the latter verdict. We had the better chances in a tight game and should have taken three of them.

Newcastle are a work in progress. There’s plenty of room for improvement but there were enough signs yesterday to suggest we’re heading in the right direction.

#2036. Why One Key Name is Missing From Parker’s Back Room Team | West Ham News

All change within West Ham’s coaching set up this week.

One name that has been mentioned by supporters since Scott Parker’s arrival, yet seems missing from the Hammers new – look post Nuno back room team is Mark Robson, with questions asked as to whether he would be involved within the new coaching set up as part of Parkers’s team.

While Robson has remained part of West Ham’s coaching structure, he actually returned to his role as the Academy of Football’s Senior Professional Development Phase Coach and Under-21s Lead Coach in the summer of 2026.

Robson did work with Nuno upon the Portuguese manager’s arrival from Nottingham Forest

According to the club, this was the same position he had previously held before stepping into first-team coaching roles. His move back to the Academy coincided with changes behind the scenes following Nuno’s decision to reshape his coaching staff in the summer, including the addition of Rui Pedro Silva, who departed earlier in the week alongside Nuno and Rui Barbosa.

When Scott Parker arrived, he too preferred to work with trusted personnel, bringing long-time colleague Jonathan Hill in as Assistant Head Coach. Yet Robson’s return to the Under-21s should never be viewed as a demotion.

The Upton Park-born coach is regarded as one of the most respected development coaches in English football. After a playing career that included helping West Ham secure promotion to the Premier League in 1992/93, Robson built an impressive coaching CV across both youth and senior football.

His biography confirms that he worked with Charlton Athletic’s academy and first team, held coaching roles at Gillingham, Peterborough United and Barnet, became an FA Youth Coach Educator, and later spent several years coaching within England’s youth international set-up. He also worked at Norwich City and Aston Villa before returning to West Ham in 2021.

Perhaps most significantly, much of that career has been centred on one thing, developing young players.

West Ham’s Academy has long prided itself on producing talent capable of making the jump into the first team. In that environment, Robson’s expertise is arguably more valuable than almost any role he could occupy elsewhere within the football club.

The situation is also not entirely new. Robson similarly returned to the Under-21s in 2024 after spending the 2023/24 campaign working within the first-team coaching set-up.

West Ham have repeatedly shown a willingness to move him between senior and academy football depending on where they feel his knowledge can have the greatest impact.

With suggestions that West Ham will continue to place significant importance on producing homegrown talent, keeping one of England’s most highly regarded youth coaches with the Under-21s may be just as important as any appointment made alongside Parker in the first-team dugout.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

I was suggesting Mark Robson as an interim manager till end of season, because he obviously gets on with this players and he has them playing quick, effective football that is good to watch. The 2nd half of WHU against Cardiff with the ball moved quickly forwards with sharp passes, reminded me of the U21 style of play.

Still think there is a need to look after ex-U21s who are around the 1st team because they still need one on one coaching, to concentrate on their weaknesses. Just a few hours a week, or individual work with a 1st team player who looks after them, or an advanced academy abroad.

I look at a player such as Fearon (he is not the only one) and I think you have the type of player who with 2-3 seasons on loan and a good club (Como with Fabregas – ain’t going to happen, but..) he would come back a very accomplished and well rounded player who would be a real asset to the club. Same for all the ex-academy lads already in the squad.

Depends on manager’s approach, coaches & Koppen, plus whoever looks after loans/ongoing ex-U21 development but important phase in their development.

Not a demotion for Mark Robson, absolutely. Working with youngsters might be what he prefers as well. A lot to do, to work on and hone. also rewarding.

#2035. Fulham 1 Newcastle 1 match ratings and comments on all Newcastle United players

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

We asked Dave Marshall to give us his match ratings and comments on individual Newcastle United players after Fulham 1 Newcastle 1.

Nail-biting. Teeth gnashing. Unease. Anxiety. Growing disapproval. Such were the rumblings of a sizable, and growing, section of Newcastle supporters as United headed to west London for a date with Fulham.

The Cottagers a side going in just two points above relegation but showing signs of life in recent weeks.

A good omen for United going in, though: winning three on the bounce in the capital this season with no goals conceded.

But pressure mounting on Matthias Jaissle and the lads after a string of bad results.

While there are both positives and negatives to take from this performance and result v Fulham…

What’s most concerning is the vibe around the club.

It was noticeable Monday at St. James’ Park. And the ranting and raving online has reached ridiculous levels of theatre.

It was good that Newcastle had an away match after capitulating twice to the Merseyside Mackems because St. James’ Park would have been too toxic to have been any support for the black and white today.

This is not the place to debate Jaissle’s tenure or his seemingly increasingly tenuous position to remain United’s gaffer.

This is not the place to criticise the personnel decisions the brass have made in recent months.

Nor is to call out any players for lack of effort, skill, finishing, passing, common sense, etc.

But it is a place to remind you that we are Newcastle United.

And United supporters have a reputation for being among the most loyal, fervent, rabid, and supportive.

50,000 strong showed up on the regular even when having to endure seasons in the Championship.

Traveling Geordies are always lauded, especially on the continent. It’s no stretch to say that a lot of club brass around England are envious of the support Newcastle gets. Supporters who bleed black-and-white.

Think 50,000 would regularly show up if one of the Septics got relegated after so many years without any trophies and Mike Ashley the club owner?

(It’s still early, but we’re on course to find out next season… but I digress.)

Face it… this is nothing compared to the dark ages of the Fat Tub of Ashley years.

The struggles of a team that lost three of its top skill players and several of its top leaders and mostly replaced them with younger, greener, and arguably less-skilled footballers?

Not the worst times United supporters have ever endured.

The learning curve of a new gaffer who’s not been on the touchline even three months yet?

Not the worst depths Geordies have suffered through.

A string of bad performances, bad results, erratic play, defensive mishaps, poor finishing in front of the net…

Not happy with MJ’s tactics or his line-ups or his substitutions or his in-game management?

But what sucks more is the vibe of the supporters right now.

It’s as if a sizable portion of the fanbase is already certain that Matthias Jaissle is a failure and this team is not worthy of support.

The schedule ramps up in quality and intensity after this international break.

So it’s time for us as United supporters to ramp up our own intensity, passion, love, and support for the black-and-white.

Come matchday, it’s time to strap on our favourite United top and do nothing but get behind the team 100%.

When the season kicked off on August 23 at home to Liverpool, pretty much no one expected United to be on 12 points and hovering mid-table after Matchday 10.

Newcastle were tagged for relegation and left for Championship dead. So it’s fair to say that United have exceeded expectations so far.

It’s also easy to forget during a long season, particularly in the midst of a spell of bad results.

Anfield and Old Trafford get all the plaudits for being difficult venues for opponents.

But those of us who live and breathe English football know, even objectively, that no set of supporters gives its team that vital push more than the rabid throngs inside a pulsating St. James’ Park.

And that’s what we have to be again to get through this.

Lukas Hornicek – 8 Bounced back after the flub v Everton on Monday. Stood tall with five saves, several of them spectacular, including early on to deny Oscar Bobb and then a last-second stop to deny Sessegnon’s laserbolt in stoppage time. Can’t be faulted on the equaliser; nothing to be done once it deflected off BDB.

Amar Dedic – 6.5 While he seemed to handle Iwobi, he struggled with Robinson’s overlapping runs. Solid in the first half as United sat back, but lagged as the match went on, his 92nd-minute yellow card invited unnecessary pressure as the draw played out.

Malick Thiaw – 7 Much-needed athleticism was back on the backline. Composed, accurate for most of his time on the pitch. Didn’t clear the ball well enough in the build up to the equaliser.

Dan Burn – 6.5 Goal disallowed due to a soft foul by Wissa. Dominant in the air, and though unlucky for Muniz’s poke to deflect off him for the equaliser, not quick enough to close down the cross that led to it. Solid partnership with Thiaw.

Lewis Hall – 7 As good as we all think Hall to be, and no doubt we’re correct, to be truly world class, he’s got to bury that 88th-minute effort, even with his non-dominant right foot. Back to his usual level for the most part, otherwise.

Sean Steur – 6.5 Good to see him back and playing with confidence. Was tidy on the ball and always looking to direct passes forward. Still not sure about him being part of a two-man midfield. Not really sure about it generally speaking, to be fair.

Nico Gonzalez – 6 Had his moments in the middle of the park, but wonder about his fitness, as he was subbed for the 2nd game in a row on the hour mark. Though he helped United keep their shape, there was no creativity to his game to break down Fulham’s low block.

Yoane Wissa – 5 Will be aggrieved with the soft foul he got called for that cancelled Burn’s would-be goal. Still, can’t put himself in position for such a call. Had a couple of opportunities but made a meal of them. Didn’t trouble the GK as much as he should have.

Jacob Murphy – 8 A screaming curler that should’ve won it and was denied an assist for Burn’s header. A Murphinho performance that United needs more consistently from him, as he was Newcastle’s most consistent threat on the break.

Harvey Barnes – 6.5 Harsh? Maybe. But when you’re an “all-he-does-is-score” kind of footballer, you’ve got to put away at least one of the three glaring chances he didn’t. He caused Fulham all types of issues but not scoring is unforgivable and it cost United two points.

William Osula – 5 Was not the beneficiary of much good service but his inconsistent effort was disappointing, Did not get a shot on goal.

Lewis Miley – 6 Came on for Nico on 61’, vital defensive header to clear a dangerous Iwobi free-kick late but hope competition with Steur will have him passing more forward. Still, good to see him back.

Joe Willock – 6 On for Wissa on 61’, he added energy dynamism to the midfield but only managed 1 SOG, and it was from long range, not too troublesome.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo – 5 On for Steur on 74’, back for the first time in weeks. Late header was saved but not too much impact. Seemed to suffer a knock in stoppage time, so hope it’s not too serious.

Anthony Elanga – N/A (On too late to rate) On for Osula on 85’, no impact in this cameo.

Fabian Schar – N/A (On too late to rate) On for Thiaw on 85’ following the equaliser to help see things out.

Matthias Jaissle – 6 Not sure that this match set-up worked, not with our cast of characters. However, Jaissle’s plan to sit deep and counter was not a bad idea, given the past couple of weeks. A sniff of desperation? Not sure, but it almost worked perfectly. However, another failure to hold the lead. You can blame MJ all you want, but it was the same last season under Howe, and with a much different cast. It’s hard to explain. But it’s got to be fixed.

The RedBird Capital founder is willing to seriously evaluate the conditions for bringing the former Southampton and Celtic man to Italy. However, to even think about landing Van Dijk, there are two key conditions to be met.

It remains to be seen if Cardinale believes this is worth it, and what the incoming Head of Football Markus Krösche might think. However, Van Dijk would be a signing capable of bringing experience, leadership, quality and personality.

#2030. Sullivan Sidelined As West Ham’s Parker Decision Revealed

Claret & Hugh can reveal today that, despite reports to the contrary, David Sullivan had no input into the decision to appoint Scott Parker as West Ham United’s new manager.

Some reports in the national media have suggested that Sullivan reacted to the Hammers’ back-to-back defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion by convincing the board to sack Nuno Espírito Santo and appoint Parker. However, information received by C&H indicates that this was not the case.

Instead, we understand that the decision was driven by West Ham chief executive Karim Virani, who, following meetings on Monday, approached the board for permission to dismiss Nuno and appoint Parker. The former Hammers midfielder was already the preferred candidate, with one club insider describing him to us today as “the perfect fit”.

And it has very much been Virani liaising with Daniel Kretinsky which has prompted the club to change direction so quickly.

Karim Virani was the driving force behind the appointment of Scott Parker

The concern surrounding Nuno’s position had been building for some time and was not simply a reaction to two disappointing results. There was growing dissatisfaction within the club over performances across a number of matches, with the defeat to West Bromwich Albion effectively proving to be the last straw.

Virani subsequently decided to act more quickly than originally anticipated, with performances showing no sign of improvement. As Claret & Hugh revealed earlier this week, Monday’s meeting brought forward a dismissal which had initially been expected to come after further consideration.

Parker was very much at the top of the list, and Virani sought the board’s approval to proceed with the change. Our latest information makes an important distinction between the board approving the appointment and Sullivan personally driving the decision.

Far from being a Sullivan-led intervention following the Southampton and West Brom defeats, C&H understands that it was Virani who took the initiative to end Nuno’s tenure and bring Parker back to West Ham.

#2029. Hammers outcasts no longer | Training hint suggests a new direction for Scott Parker’s West Ham

Blackburn Rovers await West Ham United tomorrow, with a second long trip within three days. According to local news outlets, the Irons squad is flying to Blackpool Airport this afternoon rather than endure another gruelling coach journey.

After the 450 mile midweek journey to Cardiff, going by road would have meant the West Ham teams’ tired bodies would have faced the even longer 490 mile round trip to Ewood Park – probably five hours each way – hardly the best preparation after minimal recovery.

However, a two week international break beckons during which time Scott Parker can really start to work on his tactics without the irritations of a game to interrupt his progress.

From the Hammers’ PR images released ahead of the Blackburn game, it is clear that this new broom has swept very clean in all corners of the training ground: Several players banished by Nuno are evidently now off the naughty step and, if appearances are anything to go by, are loving life under their new boss.

Maxwel Cornet, the forgotten man under successive managers, evidently got some 1:1 time with his new coach:

Presumably new West Ham manager Scott Parker is pointing out directions to the medical centre

Edson Alvarez, similarly, looks energised and content with his lot which suggests he’s in a better place now that his nemesis Nuno Espírito Santo has departed the training centre.

And one look at Alphonse Areola’s expression says it all. Training has just taken on a new dimension for the French former number three who hasn’t featured in a West Ham side since well before relegation: Parker’s chosen shot stopper at Fulham, remember.

Areola – does that smile reveal that he knows something we don’t for the starting XI tomorrow? We can but hope: I’ll wager that’s a “yes”

After Scott Parkers’ selection of a rusty Soungutou Magassa as a defensive midfielder on Wednesday, the smart money might be on another similar selection involving Magassa or Alvarez tomorrow: That would certainly account for the Mexican’s more upbeat demeanour during the training session and might even please a certain vocal selection of the fan base who have been long advancing the Mexican as the solution to the Hammers’ midfield problems.

#2024. West Ham winger has to prove the Tottenham doubters wrong – here’s how

West Ham United and Tottenham Hotspur seem to be holding their noses and doing transfer business with each other after a feud between the two club chairmen prohibited any sort of contact in well over a decade. Now that both Levy and Sullivan have departed, the two seem prepared to trade players once again.

The two sets of fans, of course, revel in player misfortune once transfers have taken place – how West Ham supporters enjoyed Mohammed Kudus’ first season travails and then merely taking £85 million from the Spuds for the signature of Mateus Fernandes and doubling our money seemed sufficient cause for satisfaction.

Quietly banking about £20 million more than the young Portuguese would generate from any other club and heading off financial armageddon with north London money seemed a deal well done.

Spurs fans now have their moment, with the gloating evident over Manor Solomon‘s failure to launch in east London. The winger has struggled despite frequent starting slots under Nuno and must now be facing competition from young Edvin Austbø who has impressed each time he’s stepped onto the turf.

As Tottenham fan site Hotspurhq.com puts it:

“West Ham are saddled with Manor Solomon, who has scored just 2 goals with 2 assists in 14 appearances. The big problem with Solomon that Tottenham have been well aware of is that he is not a team player.

Spurs had to listen to a lot of complaining from him about his minutes or about mistreatment from the club, but the real reason why he didn’t play was because he never showed he was good enough.”

Solomon – there’s a man of the match in there lurking – but many doubt he can he return to that form once again

Identifying the problem as being specifically to do with his mindset rather than his ability, the criticism goes on:

“A big part of that is Solomon does not help his teams win. He holds the ball too much and plays like someone more focused on scoring or piling up his own stats than playing with the team.”

Early on this season, after his man of the match award, there was a feeling that we’d stolen Solomon for a very modest £4 million up – front: Depending on what a decent coaching regime can coax out of the Israeli, there may still be room for quiet satisfaction.

He has the record and the ability, but needs to find a way to return to his best form. When in a Leeds eleven, he looked a top quality prospect indeed and along with Joel Piroe scored 29 times, playing no small part in taking the club back to the Premier League.

Much like his new manager, he’s done it before and knows what is needed. The jury is out as to whether he’s still got it.

#2022. Parker’s past threatens to haunt him over “dire football’ warning | West Ham News

Ask any West Ham fan after last weekend’s 3-1 home loss to West Bromwich Albion whether they’d settle for winning ways at all costs and most would have instantly nodded their agreement.

The second three goal loss at home within eight days had caused the boos to ring out as Nuno’s West Ham train derailed spectacularly, in what was to prove his last game and his ultimate undoing.

Right now there’s a relief flooding around the club as a former hero has returned to take over from negative Nuno. Long may it continue.

However the suggestions are that Parker may not prove to be the all-conquering hero that West Ham seek, judging from his impact at previous clubs. Yes, he knows how to get out of this division and yes, he sure can fix a porous defence – Burnley’s statistics speak for that.

But according to footballleagueworld.co.uk’s article this morning, his time at Burnley divided supporters with his grim, gritty style of play offering little in the way of entertainment:

“The football’s dire. He will bore you to death, and he will cause a fanbase to turn through little snide little comments. He will cause the West Ham fanbase to turn on it.

And that has happened at every single club consistently.”

Few will complain if Scott Parker gets West Ham promoted

Writes their Burnley fan columnist Aaron Wright, condemning Parker’s management style – not results – in the strongest possible terms.

“This is the biggest job he could get, if he can’t get them promoted slash win the league, and if he can’t then keep them in the Premier League, he needs to rethink pretty much everything. He is never getting a bigger job than this and his reputation as a player has helped him get this one. It’s the most guaranteed promotion you will ever have.

“The West Ham fans won’t enjoy it, but I think there’ll be a good respect to it if it turns out how Burnley’s did. 33 games unbeaten is something else.”

Which will have to be a price worth paying, simply to climb back out of this league after the mess of last season and save West Ham from the financial armageddon that not getting promoted would surely deliver.

To paraphrase Jacob Steiberg, Guardian journalist, on Parker’s football shortcomings not succeeding in the Premier League: worry about that next season – first you have to make it back.

If Wan-Bissaka is capable of playing from the substitutes' bench on Sunday, the assumption is that he will feature among the replacements.

“When I think back to where I started, it’s truly extraordinary that I can play against one of the best clubs in the world this Thursday. It’s the result of a huge amount of effort, and I’m quite proud of what I’ve achieved. I hope this journey continues for a long time to come.”

Amorim picked you out specifically as a threat to Milan. How does this make you feel? And what is your preferred role?

“Compliments are nice. It means I’m probably doing things the right way. For me, it makes no difference whether I play as a winger or a striker. In both positions, I always try to give my all and have fun on the pitch. It’s certainly significant that a coach of his calibre has mentioned me.”

Did you analyse Milan’s derby win over Inter?

“They played an intense match against Inter, and we analysed the match in detail. However, we can’t draw conclusions based on how the derby unfolded. I’m curious to see how these ninety minutes unfold.”

#2018. Veltman’s West Ham Admission Highlights Parker’s First Big Problem

West Ham defender Joël Veltman has admitted that the Hammers’ habit of starting matches poorly must change, with Scott Parker facing an immediate challenge against Blackburn Rovers this afternoon.

Speaking in an interview with the club’s official website, Veltman acknowledged that Wednesday’s disastrous first half against Cardiff City was hardly an isolated incident. West Ham recovered from three goals down to draw 3-3, but the Dutchman knows they cannot keep relying on second-half comebacks.

“It wasn’t the first time we haven’t started so well,” admitted Veltman, who wants West Ham to begin against Blackburn with the same intensity they showed after the interval in Wales.

Personally, I think West Ham’s slow starts and early capitulations are definitely a mentality problem. Nothing demonstrated that more clearly than the transformation at half-time against Cardiff, when a team that had looked completely traumatised and shell-shocked suddenly emerged looking like an entirely different side.

Of course, some of that improvement was tactical, but I’m not entirely convinced how many tactics you can impart in 15 minutes. What Parker, Mark Noble and Jarrod Bowen clearly managed to do was give the players a lift, and the difference in their attitude was extraordinary.

I’ve thought from day one that this was probably the easiest improvement any new manager could make with the current group of players. If West Ham approach matches with a positive attitude and a genuine desire to win rather than playing fearfully, I suspect much of the problem could be addressed with a decent team talk.

That doesn’t mean tactics and team selection are irrelevant, but the players have already demonstrated they possess considerably more ability than their recent performances suggest. Parker’s first job is surely to convince them of that.

Veltman himself was absolutely brilliant during the second half against Cardiff, and I think he could become an important player under Parker. His composure and positioning at right-back could allow Jarrod Bowen the freedom to drift into central areas, where the West Ham captain caused absolute havoc on Wednesday evening.

Bowen was instrumental in the comeback, and having a dependable defender behind him could make that attacking freedom much easier to accommodate. It’s another reason why I’d like to see Veltman retain his place against Blackburn.

The defender certainly recognises the opportunity ahead, telling the club: “We want to go into another away game on Saturday and start where we finished.”

That really is the challenge for Parker. West Ham don’t need to discover some previously hidden ability between now and kick-off; they need to reproduce the confidence, aggression and positive mentality they finally showed during those remarkable 45 minutes against Cardiff.

#2017. Changes forecast for Parker’s first fixture but one puzzle remains | West Ham News

Depending on which outlet you read, West Ham’s newly appointed manager plans two, three or even four changes today as the Hammers take on Blackburn Rovers with the possibility of a rise to third place beckoning depending win other results in this madcap league.

Ezra Mayers and Joel Piroe seem by all accounts to be the most likely duo to benefit from Scott Parker’s new broom. Young Mayers in particular performed creditably considering he’s had no match time since August and Morato’s clumsy performance has surely put him back onto the bench unless a centre-back is needed.

Taty Castellanos’ poor first half was contrasted by Joel Piroe’s instant impact: A pretty unanimous ‘thumbs up’ suggests Piroe will start, after assisting in one of the Irons’s three strikes on Wednesday night. Without looking a world beater, Piroe surely wins the starting place over a moody, ineffective Taty who just continues to disappoint in this league. As football fancast put it:

“Castellanos showed enough potential to create the assumption that he would walk through the Championship. To say that has not happened would be the understatement of the year.”

But the real head-scratcher is why there’s not been more noise around the goal keeper situation after Mads Hermansen let in nine goals in three successive games without laying a glove on any of the attempts.

Mads Hermansen was many people’s choice this season but he hasn’t improved on the fragility shown last year

With the existing ‘connection’ between Scott Parker and Hammers number two Alphonse Areola, most had assumed the new manager would instantly re-instate the ‘keeper who he bought to Fulham and who has been waiting, out of favour, thought this season despite Hermansen’s patchy form. The Dane was even dropped by his international side for a couple of the Nations League ties last month but still, seemingly, could do no wrong under Nuno.

Mystery solved this afternoon, perhaps, when the side is announced. I’m sure most Irons supporters would rather see Areola at the top of the team sheet: No doubt a little rusty but more confidence-inspiring than his counterpart.

#2015. Blackburn Rovers 0 – 0 West Ham United | Half time report

A cold crisp afternoon, perfect for football saw West Ham seemingly doing their best to get into their opponent’s half after the last three weeks’ slow, ponderous starts. The Hammers spent the early moments camped in Blackburn’s half, accompanied by the noise of 7000 visiting fans making Ewood Park sound more like London Stadium on a good day.

Most of West Ham’s early movement was through Mayers and Austbø down the left, the two combining well with the full back pushed right forward in an adventurous set up by Scott Parker.

However it was Blackburn who almost struck first thanks to an overlap down their right and a shot that looped agonisingly over Hermansens’ goal. Mayers responded by fizzing one cross just out of reach of Piroe -nil nil at 20 minutes.

Engels, Austbo and Mayers combined well as the Hammers attacked repeatedly down Blackburn’s left, Austbø impressing in place of Solomon. Half an hour gone and few scares for West Ham:  A more competitive, aggressive start than in recent weeks. Piroe had one ball played through but his lack of pace allowed defenders to crowd him out.

The half continued in the same vein, West Ham looking well capable of scoring with most of the attacking coming down the flanks, Mayers on the overlap giving Scott Parker a new dimension to his Hammers offensive work.

Worryingly, Engels went over on his ankle just on the stroke of half time –  the teams went in at 0 – 0, a far more measured, controlled half than West Ham fans have been treated to in recent weeks.

#2014. Blackburn Rovers 2 – 1 West Ham United | Final whistle, first impressions as new manager bounce falls flat

West Ham managed to overturn their recent sequence of dreadful, lethargic starts with bright first half performance against Blackburn Rovers. Both sides had their chances but West Ham’s attack dominated the first half, largely through Austbø and Ezra Mayers down the left hand side.

The Hammers set up with Engels the deepest midfielder sitting in front of the back four and Kanté plus Mukasa the more forward of the trio. It seemed to protect the back line a little better as, apart from one looped shot over Hermansen’s goal, Blackburn’s threat was contained during the first 45 minutes.

Three or four times in the first ’45 Mayers overlapped after combining with Austbø – looking far more potent a threat than Solomon who he’d replaced – and got excellent crosses in from the left, an attacking option that had been lacking with Morato as the full back.

Piroe headed against the post early in the second half after Austbo – again – twisted and turned on the left, and Engles crashed the rebound just wide. Waves of pressure developed on the Blackburn goal as the Hammers responded to their half time talk but against the run of play from a break down the other end, Blackburn took the lead through Gudjohnson who headed through Hermansen’s legs. West Ham behind again.

Parker responded with Solomon for Austbø who’d run his socks off for an hour and Taty appearing in place of Kanté.

Controversy as Rovers scored a second with Kilman prostrate after a head collision – Dapo Afolayan the ex West Ham boy fired one into the corner leaving West Ham with a mountain to climb. It must be said, naive defending from West Ham.

Joel Piroe grabbed one back after a lucky bounce sat nicely for him in the box: 2 – 1 with eight minutes to go and the Ewood Park atmosphere changed, the home fans nervy and the Hammers fans in full voice. The minutes ticked away and West Ham struggled to get the ball towards Blackburn’s box: Orford, a late substitute, very fortunate to avoid conceding a penalty in the closing minutes – once again the lack of VAR coming to West Ham’s rescue.

Five minutes of added time, West Ham looking as if they had neither the urgency or the ability to surge forward again, fiddling about on the edge of their own box with Hermansen being booed every time he touched the ball. One last chance as Soucek headed straight at the ‘keeper in the last few seconds and that was that. Poor. Very poor. So much possession and so little to show for it.

#2013. Player Ratings: Blackburn 2-1 West Ham as Hermansen Has a Nightmare

West Ham’s promising start at Ewood Park ultimately counted for very little as Scott Parker’s side slipped to a 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers. Despite enjoying plenty of possession and creating opportunities, the Hammers were undone by poor defending and some particularly questionable goalkeeping.

Joël Piroe’s late goal gave West Ham a chance of rescuing something, but the longer the game went on, the worse we seemed to play. There were some decent individual performances, particularly early on, but others will want to forget this afternoon in a hurry.

A really poor afternoon for the goalkeeper. I thought he could have been far more commanding for Blackburn’s opening goal, whether that meant catching the cross, punching it or simply getting something on the ball. He did make a straightforward late save from Todd Cantwell, but that doesn’t change my overall assessment.

One of West Ham’s more reliable performers before being substituted. Made some useful defensive interceptions and regularly pushed forward to support Bowen down the right. Tried a couple of long throws into the penalty area, although they didn’t really cause Blackburn much trouble.

Had some positive moments going forward, including a driving run from defence and a header that went narrowly wide early in the second half. However, I thought he could have done better for Blackburn’s first goal, and his performance deteriorated badly towards the end. Was fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping twice during a dreadful passage of play that handed Blackburn a dangerous counter-attack.

Probably West Ham’s most dependable defender on the day. Made several important interceptions, particularly down the left where Blackburn repeatedly threatened, and was willing to carry the ball forward to help build attacks. Also produced a decent cross for Castellanos, although the resulting header went wide.

A mixed afternoon for the youngster. I was impressed with his willingness to get forward, his passing combinations with Austbø and some of the crosses he delivered. However, Blackburn repeatedly targeted his side, often leaving him facing two opponents, and he was beaten too easily in the build-up to the opening goal. Still very much learning the position.

Didn’t think he had a particularly good game. Had plenty of involvement, took the corners and got himself into shooting positions, but too often the final product was disappointing. Lost possession unnecessarily on occasions, failed to close down Blackburn’s second goalscorer quickly enough and wasted a promising late free kick with poor delivery.

You certainly couldn’t fault his work rate. At times he seemed to be everywhere, covering at left-back, appearing on the right and getting forward to support the attack. However, he wasn’t nearly as influential on the ball as he had been during the second half against Cardiff, and his shooting was disappointing. Replaced by Castellanos after 64 minutes.

One of West Ham’s more inventive players, particularly during the first half. Looked to move the ball quickly, attempted some clever through passes and wasn’t afraid to shoot, forcing one save and seeing another effort deflected behind. Not everything worked, but at least he was trying to make things happen.

I was genuinely surprised when he was substituted because he’d been one of West Ham’s livelier attacking players. Produced a lovely dribble past two defenders in the first half, linked up well with Mayers and delivered an excellent cross that Bowen headed against the post. Could perhaps have offered Mayers more defensive protection before Blackburn’s opener, but I thought he was contributing plenty going forward.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

Worked hard to make things happen and was heavily involved in West Ham’s attacking play, particularly from the right. Unlucky to see his header strike the post following Austbø’s cross, while a difficult chance from close range went wide as he was falling and sliding. Also produced a lovely chipped delivery for Souček’s late header, but couldn’t quite provide the decisive contribution West Ham needed.

A frustrating performance rescued to some extent by an excellent goal. Too often he seemed hesitant in promising positions, allowing defenders to recover, while one particularly poor pass in the second half wasted a good attacking opportunity. However, he reacted brilliantly to Castellanos’ cross in the 82nd minute, firing high into the roof of the net. Whatever else you say about his performance, he took that chance extremely well.

Replaced Austbø after 58 minutes and was practically anonymous. Considering how involved Austbø had been, the substitution certainly didn’t improve West Ham’s attacking threat down the left.

Introduced for Kanté after 64 minutes and provided the cross that led to Piroe’s goal. Also had a header go wide from a Kilman delivery and was involved in the scramble that presented Bowen with a difficult chance. At least contributed something tangible to the attack.

Didn’t have a great deal of time to influence proceedings, particularly with West Ham having already lost their shape. Played one very silly ball into Orford inside our own penalty area, creating unnecessary danger. However, he also got into one of those familiar goalscoring positions in stoppage time, only to direct his header straight at the goalkeeper from Bowen’s excellent delivery.

Another substitute who came into a team that had lost its shape and was struggling for confidence. Was put in a difficult position by Souček’s poor pass inside the penalty area and was fortunate not to concede a penalty. Difficult to judge him too harshly given the limited time he had on the pitch and the state of the game when he entered.

#2012. Blackburn Rovers 2- 1 West Ham | Boos and ironic cheers highlight massive concern

THERE was an ironic cheer from the West Ham away supporters at about 88 minutes, which considering their team was 2- 1 down and looking clueless was even more remarkable.

The cheer was for Mads Hermansen finally making a save, with a shot hit straight at him being pretty much the first time he’d connected with anything, as another two goals had found their way under and past the hapless Dane.

7000 West Ham fans had made the trip to Blackburn in expectation of a triumphant start to Parker’s era and yet saw their starting eleven dominate the ball but fail to score. Hermansen had dealt with a smattering of booing from his own fans ever since Rovers took the lead with a header that went between the Dane’s legs.

Times’ up, Mads. The big concern was that Scott Parker picked him ahead of Areola. We told him….

Hardly a confidence boost for the young keeper who surely should not have been selected in the first place.

No criticism through could be attached to Hermansen for Blackburn’s second goal but West Ham found themselves two goals behind, chasing the game and seemingly nothing to offer, back passing and fiddling around in the last few minutes.

Parker can have no excuse now for continuing to select his hapless keeper. The Dane plays as if he’s got arthritic knees (take it fromm one who knows) and doesn’t dive for anything, just collapsing to the left or right, week after week.

Whatever issue there may be with second-in-line Alphonse Areola, he simply has to start after the international break.

Otherwise, we may as well simply drape a goal keeper’s jersey on the cross bar: It’ll be about as effective.

The most frustrating thing? We called this, as did just about every West Ham fan: Hermansen is just not good enough.
